title: Combinational Logic Circuits

chunks.summary: SOP expressions are AND terms ORed together; POS expressions are OR terms ANDed together. Every combinational circuit can be expressed in either canonical form.
chunks.text: A Sum-Of-Products (SOP) expression consists of two or more AND (product) terms that are ORed together, e.g. z = AB + AC + BC. Each product term is implemented with an AND gate, and the terms are combined with a single OR gate, so any SOP expression maps directly onto a two-level AND-OR circuit. The Product-Of-Sums (POS) form is the dual: two or more OR (sum) terms are ANDed together, e.g. z = (A+B)(A+C)(B+C). Each sum term is implemented with an OR gate, and the terms are combined with a single AND gate. SOP is by far the more commonly used form in this course because truth tables and Karnaugh maps naturally produce SOP expressions (one product term per row where the output is 1).

chunks.summary: Logic circuits are simplified by first expanding the expression into SOP form (using DeMorgan's theorems to break down inversion bars), then factoring out common terms; the worked example z = ABC + AB(A'C)' simplifies to z = A(C+B).
chunks.text:
Simplifying a logic circuit reduces the number of gates (and gate inputs) needed to implement the same function, which lowers cost, power, and propagation delay. The two main simplification tools are Boolean algebra (algebraic manipulation) and Karnaugh mapping (graphical). 

Algebraic simplification procedure: (1) Write the output expression directly from the circuit. (2) Put the expression into SOP form by applying DeMorgan's theorems to break down large inversion (overbar) signs spanning multiple variables, then multiply out all the resulting terms. (3) Inspect the SOP expression for common factors among the product terms; factoring out a common factor eliminates one or more terms/gates.

Worked example from the slides: starting from a circuit whose output is z = ABC + AB * (A'C)'. Applying DeMorgan to (A'C)' gives A + C', so z = ABC + AB(A + C'). Multiplying out: z = ABC + ABA + ABC'. Since ABA = AB (X*X=X), this becomes z = ABC + AB + ABC'. The first and third terms share the common factor AC (specifically ABC and ABC' both contain A and B, and differ only in C vs C'), so factoring: z = AB(C + C') + AB = AB(1) + AB... The slides' own factoring path is: the 1st and 3rd terms have AC in common and are factored out, and since B + B' = 1 the two C-terms collapse, then A is factored out of what remains, yielding the final simplified result z = A(C + B). This drops the circuit from three AND gates + inverters + an OR gate down to a single 2-input OR gate feeding a single 2-input AND gate (A ANDed with (C+B)) — a much simpler circuit that is functionally identical to the original for every input combination.
chunks.figure_note: Pages 5, 7, and 9 show the original (unsimplified) gate-level circuit for z = ABC + AB(A'C)' built from AND/OR/NOT gates, and page 9 shows the simplified circuit z = A(C+B) (one 2-input OR gate whose output and A feed a 2-input AND gate). The slides state circuit (b), the simplified one, is 'clearly less complex' than circuit (a). Exact gate layout/wire routing not visually re-verified (PDF renderer unavailable in this environment) but the boolean derivation was checked algebraically.

chunks.topic: Designing Combinational Logic Circuits from a Truth Table
chunks.summary: The standard design procedure is: build a truth table from the problem statement, write one AND term per row where the output is 1, OR those terms together (SOP), simplify, then implement as AND gates feeding a single OR gate.
chunks.text:
To design a combinational logic circuit from a word problem or specification, follow this procedure: (1) Interpret the problem statement and set up a truth table listing every input combination and the required output. (2) For each row where the output is required to be 1, write the corresponding AND (product) term — a variable appears uncomplemented in the term if it is 1 in that row, complemented if it is 0. (3) Combine (OR) all these product terms to form the SOP expression for the output — this is guaranteed correct because it reproduces the truth table exactly (one term is uniquely '1' for each 1-output row and 0 otherwise). (4) Simplify the SOP expression algebraically or with a K-map if possible. (5) Implement the final simplified expression: each remaining product term becomes an AND gate, and all the AND-gate outputs feed a single OR gate.

Worked example: design a 3-input (A,B,C) majority circuit whose output is HIGH only when a majority (at least two) of the inputs are HIGH. The truth table has output=1 for rows ABC = 011, 101, 110, 111. The unsimplified SOP is z = A'BC + AB'C + ABC' + ABC. Factoring/grouping common pairs (each pair of minterms that differ in one variable combines, e.g. ABC + ABC' = AB, ABC + AB'C = AC, ABC + A'BC = BC) simplifies this to z = AB + AC + BC, which requires only 3 two-input AND gates and one 3-input OR gate instead of 4 three-input AND gates and one 4-input OR gate.
chunks.figure_note: Page 10 shows a small circuit whose output is 1 only for A=0,B=1 (2-input case). Pages 12-13 show the 3-input majority-circuit truth table with the AND term written next to each output=1 row. Page 14 shows the simplified 3-input majority circuit (three 2-input AND gates -> one 3-input OR gate). Layout not visually re-verified (renderer unavailable) but the truth table and simplification were checked by hand.

chunks.summary: A K-map is a graphical grid arranged so adjacent cells differ in only one variable; looping adjacent groups of 1s (pairs, quads, octets, with wraparound) and reading the common, unchanging variables in each loop produces a minimal SOP expression.
chunks.text:
The Karnaugh map (K-map) is a graphical method for simplifying a Boolean expression or truth table. It is theoretically usable for any number of variables but practically limited to about 5-6 variables (beyond that, computer minimization tools like Quine-McCluskey are used instead). Truth-table output values are placed into map cells: a 2-variable map has 4 cells, a 4-variable map has 16 cells. The defining property of a K-map's layout (Gray-code ordering of row/column labels) is that any two horizontally or vertically ADJACENT cells differ in exactly one variable.

SOP simplification procedure: (1) Construct the K-map and place a 1 in every cell corresponding to a truth-table row where the output is 1 (0s or don't-cares elsewhere). (2) Loop any isolated 1s that are not adjacent to any other 1 (each becomes its own full product term). (3) Loop 1s that occur only in pairs. (4) Loop octets (groups of 8 adjacent 1s) first among the larger groupings, even if some of those 1s were already looped, because larger loops give simpler terms. (5) Loop quads (groups of 4) that contain at least one 1 not already covered by a larger loop. (6) Loop any remaining necessary pairs to cover 1s not yet included in a loop. (7) Form the final SOP expression as the OR-sum of the term generated by each loop. Looping can wrap around the top/bottom edges and the left/right edges of the map (the map is topologically a torus).

Within each loop, any variable that appears in BOTH its complemented and uncomplemented form across the cells of that loop is eliminated from the term (because it doesn't affect whether those cells are all 1); only variables that stay the same (same true/complement form) across every cell of the loop appear in the resulting product term. Bigger loops eliminate more variables and give simpler (fewer-literal) terms: a loop of 2 eliminates 1 variable, a loop of 4 eliminates 2 variables, a loop of 8 eliminates 3 variables.
chunks.figure_note: Page 15 shows a 2-variable K-map with truth-table values placed in it. Page 16 shows a full 4-variable K-map grid (4x4, Gray-code row/column labels) with 1s placed from a truth table. Page 17 illustrates looping of a pair (group of 2), a quad (group of 4), and an octet (group of 8) of adjacent 1s. Page 18-19 illustrate wraparound looping between the top/bottom and left/right edges. Exact cell values on these example maps were not visually re-verified since the PDF page-render tool is unavailable here; the looping RULES stated above are transcribed accurately from the slide text and are standard/verifiable K-map theory.

chunks.summary: XOR outputs HIGH only when its two inputs differ (x = AB' + A'B); XNOR outputs HIGH only when its two inputs are equal (x = AB + A'B'). Both are available as dedicated quad-gate ICs and are used e.g. to compare two bits for equality.
chunks.text:
The Exclusive-OR (XOR) gate produces a HIGH output only when its two inputs are at opposite logic levels: x = AB' + A'B. A shorthand notation uses a circled-plus symbol (x = A XOR B, written A(+)B in ASCII here) to represent this expression. XOR always has exactly two inputs (larger XOR trees are built by cascading 2-input XOR gates). Dedicated quad-XOR ICs exist across logic families: 74LS86 (TTL/LS), 74C86 (CMOS), 74HC86 (high-speed CMOS) — each package holds four independent 2-input XOR gates.

The Exclusive-NOR (XNOR) gate is the complement of XOR: it produces a HIGH output only when its two inputs are at the SAME logic level: x = AB + A'B'. XOR and XNOR outputs are always opposite of each other for the same inputs. Dedicated quad-XNOR ICs: 74LS266 (TTL/LS), 74C266 (CMOS), 74HC266 (high-speed CMOS).

A classic application is a 2-bit equality comparator/detector: feeding each corresponding pair of bits from two 2-bit numbers into an XNOR gate, then ANDing the two XNOR outputs together, produces a single output that is HIGH only when the two 2-bit numbers are identical (this generalizes to any bit width by ANDing all the per-bit XNOR outputs).
chunks.figure_note: Pages 21 and 24 show the standard XOR and XNOR internal gate circuits (built from AND/OR/NOT gates) alongside their 2-input truth tables. Page 26 shows a 2-bit equality-detector circuit built from two XNOR gates feeding an AND gate, with its truth table. Circuit topology described from slide captions; not pixel-verified since page-image rendering is unavailable here.

chunks.summary: An enable/disable circuit uses one or more control inputs to allow (enable) or block (disable) an input signal from reaching the output; common building blocks pass a signal only when a specific control condition is met.
chunks.text:
Enable/disable circuits are extremely common in digital design. A circuit is ENABLED when it allows an input signal to pass through to the output, and DISABLED when it blocks that signal, forcing the output to a fixed level (HIGH or LOW depending on design) regardless of the input.

Example 1: a circuit that passes a signal to the output only when two control inputs B and C are BOTH HIGH; otherwise the output stays LOW. This is implemented by ANDing the signal with the enable condition (e.g., output = signal * B * C).

Example 2: a circuit that passes a signal only when exactly one (but not both) of two control inputs is HIGH — otherwise the output stays HIGH. This is an XOR-based or gated design where the disable condition forces a HIGH rather than a LOW output.

Example 3: a routing/steering circuit with signal input A, control input B, and two outputs X and Y: when B=1, X follows A and Y is forced to 0; when B=0, X is forced to 0 and Y follows A. This is a 1-to-2 demultiplexer built from AND gates: X = A*B, Y = A*B'.
chunks.figure_note: Page 29 shows the AND-gated circuit passing a signal only when B AND C are both HIGH. Page 30 shows the circuit that passes the signal only when exactly one of two control inputs is HIGH (output otherwise HIGH). Page 31 shows the 1-input/1-control/2-output steering circuit (X=A*B, Y=A*B'). Gate-level detail summarized from slide captions; not visually re-verified since PDF rendering is unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Basic Characteristics of Digital ICs (packaging, TTL vs CMOS, floating inputs)
chunks.summary: Digital ICs are fabricated on a semiconductor substrate and housed in packages such as DIP or PLCC; ICs are categorized as bipolar (TTL, using NPN/PNP transistors) or unipolar (CMOS, using FETs); unused/floating inputs behave differently and must be tied off for CMOS to avoid damage.
chunks.text:
An IC 'chip' consists of resistors, diodes, and transistors fabricated on a semiconductor substrate, and ICs are often categorized by complexity based on the number of gates they contain (SSI, MSI, LSI, etc.). The Dual-In-line Package (DIP) has two parallel rows of pins and was the most common package in older equipment; pins are numbered counterclockwise viewed from the top, starting next to an identifying notch or dot. The actual silicon die inside a DIP is much smaller than the package (roughly 0.05" square) and is connected to the package pins by extremely fine (about 1-mil diameter) bond wires. The PLCC (Plastic Leaded Chip Carrier) is a more modern package using J-shaped leads that curl under the IC body, allowing a smaller footprint.

ICs are also categorized by transistor technology: Bipolar ICs (the TTL family) use NPN and PNP bipolar junction transistors; Unipolar ICs (the CMOS family) use field-effect transistors (FETs). The TTL family has several subfamilies (74, 74LS, 74S, 74ALS, 74F, etc.) that differ mainly in power dissipation and switching speed while sharing the same pinouts and logic functions. The CMOS family (74C, 74HC, 74HCT, etc.) performs equivalent logic functions but is not always pin-for-pin compatible with TTL.

An input that is not connected to anything is 'floating.' A floating TTL input behaves like (and measures near) a logic HIGH. A floating CMOS input, by contrast, is high-impedance and can pick up noise, potentially causing erratic switching, excess current, overheating, and even permanent device damage — so unused CMOS inputs should always be tied to a definite HIGH or LOW level (best practice for both families, though critical for CMOS). Voltages that fall in the 'indeterminate range' between valid LOW and valid HIGH thresholds give unpredictable circuit behavior and should always be avoided.

A connection/schematic diagram documents every electrical connection: pin numbers, IC part numbers, component values, signal names, and supply voltages, so any point in a multi-IC circuit can be referenced unambiguously (e.g. modern tools like Quartus II schematic capture generate such diagrams).

Page 41 shows a logic-level voltage chart comparing valid LOW/HIGH ranges and the indeterminate region for TTL vs CMOS. Page 42 shows a multi-IC connection diagram with pin numbers labeled at each gate. Page 43 is a Quartus II schematic-capture screenshot. chunks.topic: Troubleshooting Digital Systems: Internal and External Faults
chunks.summary: Troubleshooting proceeds through fault detection, isolation, and correction using tools like a logic probe, oscilloscope, and logic pulser; internal IC faults include shorted/open pins, while external faults include open/shorted signal lines, faulty power supplies, and output loading.
chunks.text:
Troubleshooting a faulty digital circuit follows three basic steps: (1) Fault detection — compare the circuit's actual operation to its expected operation to confirm a fault exists. (2) Fault isolation — use test/measurement tools to narrow down exactly where the fault is. (3) Fault correction — repair (e.g. replace) the faulty component. The basic troubleshooting tools are the logic probe (indicates presence/absence/level of a signal at a pin), the oscilloscope (shows waveforms over time), and the logic pulser (injects test pulses).

Internal IC faults (Section 4-11) are commonly one of: (a) internal circuit malfunction causing outputs that don't respond properly or are unpredictable; (b) an input or output internally shorted to ground or VCC, which forces that pin permanently LOW or HIGH; (c) an internally open-circuited input or output — an open output floats (reads an indeterminate/erratic level), and a floating TTL input behaves as HIGH while a floating CMOS input can behave erratically or destructively; (d) an internal short between two (non-power) pins, which forces the two pins' signals to always be identical, often producing a voltage with three distinct levels when the driving signals disagree.

External faults (Section 4-12) include: open signal lines (broken wire, poor solder/wire-wrap connection, cracked PCB trace, bent/broken IC pin, faulty socket) — detectable visually or with an ohmmeter; shorted signal lines (sloppy wiring, solder bridges, incomplete PCB etching) causing two nets — possibly including VCC or ground — to be electrically tied together, also detectable visually/with an ohmmeter; faulty power supply — ICs operate erratically or not at all if supply voltage is out of range, unregulated, ungrounded, or has AC ripple (verify with a scope and DMM at each suspect IC); and output loading — connecting too many gate inputs to one output exceeds its rated fan-out/output current, pulling the output voltage into the indeterminate range (usually a symptom of poor design or a wiring mistake).
chunks.figure_note: Page 45 shows a logic-probe indication chart (probe response for HIGH/LOW/pulsing/floating pins). Pages 47-50 show pairs of small circuits illustrating internally-shorted-to-ground vs internally-shorted-to-VCC faults on inputs and outputs, and shorted-together-pins behavior. Page 52 shows a worked troubleshooting example with a NOR gate whose indeterminate output is traced to an indeterminate input at pin 2 (fed from another IC's pin 6, labeled Z1-6/Z2-2). Diagrams summarized from captions; not visually re-verified since PDF rendering is unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Programmable Logic Devices (PLDs) and Hierarchical/Top-Down Design
chunks.summary: PLDs contain a large, electronically-configurable array of gates (a programmable switch matrix) that can be programmed in-system or out-of-system from software; complex systems are designed hierarchically/top-down, defining and testing sub-blocks before combining them.
chunks.text:
A Programmable Logic Device (PLD) contains a large number of logic gates on a single IC whose interconnections are configured electronically rather than fixed at fabrication. This lets the design process be automated: designers specify inputs, outputs, and the logical relationship between them, and development software electronically configures the PLD's internal switch matrix (programmable array) to realize that logic — deciding which row/column intersections in the matrix are connected programs how inputs route to outputs.

PLDs can be programmed out-of-system (removed and placed in a dedicated hardware programmer connected to a PC, whose software translates and loads the configuration) or in-system (programmed while still installed in the target system, via an interface cable connected to dedicated 'portal' pins, driven by PC software).

Logic circuits destined for a PLD can be described via schematic diagrams, logic equations, truth tables, or an HDL (AHDL, VHDL); development software (e.g. historically Altera MAX+PLUS II, and its successor Quartus II) translates any of these description styles into the 1s and 0s that configure the device, and can simulate the design's timing before programming actual hardware.

Hierarchical design builds a system from small, individually-designed and individually-tested logic blocks that are combined into larger sections, which are in turn combined into the complete system. Top-down design starts by defining the system's major subsections, then further defines the individual circuits that make up each subsection — so the overall system is decomposed from the top down, while (in a bottom-up implementation flow) each low-level block is designed, compiled, and simulator-verified before being combined upward and finally programmed into a PLD for final verification. This hierarchical/top-down approach lets each level of the design be tested independently before integration, catching errors early.
chunks.figure_note: Page 57 depicts a programmable switch-matrix grid showing which row/column intersections are 'connected' vs left open to program the routing. Page 63 shows an HDL timing-simulation waveform screenshot. Page 64 shows a bottom-up flow diagram: design file -> compile -> simulate -> program PLD -> verify. chunks.topic: Representing Data and Truth Tables in HDL (AHDL/VHDL bit vectors)
chunks.summary: HDLs use prefixed literals/scalars for number systems and named bit arrays (vectors) with an index range to represent multi-bit ports and signals; truth tables can be entered directly as HDL constructs in both AHDL and VHDL.
chunks.text:
Every HDL (and programming language) has its own convention for writing literal numbers in different bases, typically using a prefix to indicate the number system (e.g. binary, hex). These are called scalars or literals and must be read as symbols representing an underlying binary bit pattern, not as the base-10 value directly.

To describe a port carrying more than one bit, a name is given along with a bit count, forming a bit array (bit vector). Each bit (element) of the vector has a unique index (e.g. 0 through 7 for an 8-bit vector) identifying its position — both HDLs and general-purpose programming languages use this array-indexing convention.

VHDL syntax: a bit-vector port is declared inside the ENTITY's PORT clause with its name, mode (IN/OUT/INOUT), type, and index range in parentheses, e.g. `PORT (p1 : IN BIT_VECTOR (7 DOWNTO 0));` declares an 8-bit input port named p1. Inside the ARCHITECTURE section, intermediate values can be declared as SIGNALs of type BIT_VECTOR with their own range, e.g. `SIGNAL temp : BIT_VECTOR (7 DOWNTO 0); ... temp <= p1;` connects all 8 bits of p1 to temp in one assignment. When no specific bit indices are given, the entire vector is connected; individual bits can instead be connected by indexing (e.g. p1(3)) inside parentheses. VHDL also provides standardized data types and macrofunctions (device descriptions, common functions) via libraries, avoiding the need to redefine common building blocks from scratch.

Truth tables can be entered directly in either AHDL or VHDL as a construct that lists each input combination and its corresponding output(s), which the compiler then synthesizes into gate-level logic — this gives designers a way to specify combinational logic exactly the way it's specified on paper, without manually deriving a Boolean equation first.

chunks.topic: Decision Control Structures in HDL: IF/THEN/ELSE, ELSIF, and CASE
chunks.summary: HDL decision structures let a design branch based on conditions: IF/THEN for a single conditional action, IF/THEN/ELSE for a two-way choice, ELSIF (chained IF/ELSE) for many mutually-exclusive outcomes, and CASE for matching one of several discrete values of an expression.
chunks.text:
IF/THEN provides a framework for a single conditional action: it is used when there is a choice between doing something (if the condition is true) and doing nothing (if false). IF/THEN/ELSE extends this to a two-way choice: one action executes if the condition is true, and a different (ELSE) action executes if it is false.

By chaining together multiple IF/ELSE decisions, an ELSIF (else-if) structure is formed, which evaluates a sequence of conditions in order; as each condition is evaluated, the matching action is performed if true, otherwise evaluation proceeds to the next condition — this implements a choice among many possible outcomes. Example: a temperature-measuring system fed by an A/D converter uses ELSIF logic — IF the digital value is <= 8, light only 'Too Cold'; ELSE IF the value is > 8 AND < 11, light only 'Just Right'; ELSE light only 'Too Hot'.

The CASE construct evaluates the value of a single expression/object and then compares it against a list of possible values (cases), executing the action associated with whichever case matches. It differs from IF/ELSIF in that only one branch is ever matched/executed for a given case statement (a cleaner style when there are many discrete, mutually-exclusive possibilities rather than a chain of inequality comparisons). Example: a vending-machine coin detector receives three digital signals (Q for quarter, D for dime, N for nickel), each asserted only when the corresponding coin is detected; a CASE statement (or equivalent decision structure) maps the active input signal to a binary number representing that coin's value, to be used elsewhere in the circuit (e.g. for a running total).
